meeting_header:
Date: 2026-11-30 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m
Redwood: Ava Chen (AE), Diego Morales (SE)
Helios: Maya Singh (Platform), Liam O'Connor (Cloud), Priya Rao (Security), Tom Baker (CTO)
transcript:
00:00 Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll do a deep dive on private VPC networking and how our runtime behaves under different network patterns. i'm Ava, AE at Redwood. Diego's our SE. 00:15 Diego (Redwood SE): Hi all, quick agenda: private control plane connectivity (PrivateLink/private link vs peering), egress for model pulls, DNS and split horizon, then runtime performance: latency, KV cache behavior, batching, quantization tradeoffs. 00:30 Maya (Helios): Sounds good. high level constraint: our infra is in a locked down AWS org, admin doesn't want any internet-facing endpoints. we prefer PrivateLink or TGW. 00:45 Liam (Helios): We use Transit Gateway for most cross-account traffic, but TGW attachments require approvals and we want to compare PrivateLink first. 00:50 Priya (Helios Security): SOC2 concerns - we need audit logs, KMS integration, and ability to rotate keys. also SSO with SAML. 01:05 Diego: Understood. For Private VPC we support two models: 1) Private control plane over PrivateLink - Redwood exposes a PrivateLink endpoint service; customer creates an interface endpoint in their VPC, traffic to control plane stays within AWS; or 2) VPC Peering / Transit Gateway for data plane if customer prefers lower latency for high throughput. 01:25 Tom (CTO): What's the latency delta between PrivateLink and peering? is PrivateLink adding overhead? 01:35 Diego: Good question. PrivateLink adds a small hop, typical extra RTT is ~1-2 ms in same region depending on AZ hops. More important is whether data plane traffic crosses NAT or internet - that would add much more. 01:50 Ava: Also worth noting the control plane is low-bandwidth (config, orchestration). The heavy token traffic (inference byte streams) stays on the data plane between Redwood runtime and customer's workers when using Dedicated/Private deployments with peering or TGW. 02:05 Maya: If we use PrivateLink for control plane, how do model pulls happen? We need our nodes to pull container images or model artifacts from S3/ecr. That typically requires egress. 02:15 Diego: Right - model artifact pulls need outbound connectivity to S3/ECR endpoints. Options: 1) use VPC endpoints (gateway endpoints) for S3, ECR; 2) NAT gateway with egress via your NAT; 3) host artifacts in a customer-accessible internal repo. We usually recommend gateway endpoints for S3 to avoid NAT. 02:35 Liam: We prefer gateway endpoints. we'd also like to avoid cross-account IAM complexity; can Redwood pull artifacts if we provide a presigned URL? 02:45 Ava: Presigned URLs are an option for initial POC; for production we'd prefer cross-account roles with limited scopes or replicating artifacts to a Redwood-managed bucket via secure transfer. 03:00 Priya: On DNS, our infra uses split-horizon private hosted zones. how does PrivateLink endpoint resolve? 03:10 Diego: PrivateLink uses interface ENIs - you'll point your private hosted zone to the endpoint DNS name. sometimes the auto-generated endpoint DNS names are unintuitive, and yes you may need a Route53 private hosted zone entry or conditional forwarders. 03:25 Maya: Noted, we have strict route tables and NACLs. what security groups are required on the interface endpoint? 03:35 Diego: We need to allow outbound from your runtime subnet to the PrivateLink endpoint's ENIs on TLS(443). For data plane peering/TGW you need security rules allowing traffic between your subnets and Redwood's service subnets on the ports used by the runtime (443 for control, gRPC typically 443/80 or configured port for internal runtime). 03:55 Ava: Quick note about mTLS - we support mutual TLS between control plane and customer agents; that can be required for higher security posture. 04:05 Priya: Good. Also, audit logs - can we get request-level logs and model prompt traces? 04:12 Diego: We provide audit logs and can stream to your CloudWatch/Cloud Storage via log forwarder or S3 bucket subscription, but we can redact PII before shipping if needed. We'll include SOC2 docs in the security pack. 04:30 Tom: On runtime perf: our main KPI is p95 latency for single-turn generation under 512 tokens. We're seeing targets of sub-200ms p95 for qps ~5. how does Redwood's Private runtime behave? 04:45 Diego: Several knobs: batching window, continuous batching, KV cache hit rate, and quantization profile. In-place numbers (subject to workload): with no network overhead, a 70B dense model in fp16 on A100s with optimized kernels we can get ~60-120 ms per-token autoreg depending on prompt; but generation p95 depends on batching and concurrency. 05:10 Maya: What about quantization? We want to use int8 or 4-bit to save memory - how does that affect latency and accuracy? 05:20 Diego: Quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput due to better cache locality; latency per token can improve slightly, but there can be model-specific quality regressions. We suggest running eval prompt sets. For some models int8 gives similar latency but small accuracy delta; 4-bit aggressive quant gives more variance. Diego: Also, our runtime supports mixed quant paths - KV cache stays in optimized format, and we have kernel fallbacks. 05:45 Liam: KV cache - can it be persisted across requests or across pods? 05:52 Diego: KV cache is per runtime instance. For pinned long-running sessions we keep KV in memory; for scale-out we warm caches via prefix caching or we use a centralized cache for replicated sessions (but that adds network hop). Typically we recommend keeping critical low-latency sessions on warm pinned instances. 06:10 Maya: How does batching interact with p95? we don't want batching windows that hurt tail latency. 06:15 Diego: We have adaptive batching - max wait window defaults to 20ms in low-latency mode; for throughput-heavy use you can increase to 50-150ms. Also continuous batching (tokens accumulate) helps throughput but can increase p95. There's an option for priority routing: low-latency requests bypass batching or go to a low-batch pool. 06:35 Ava: For the POC we can run two profiles: low-latency (20ms window, 1-2 concurrency) and throughput (50-100ms window, high concurrency) and report p50/p95/p99. 06:45 Tom: Sounds good. also curious about network serialization overhead for kv lookups if we used a remote cache. 06:52 Diego: If using remote KV, each lookup adds RTT. If your intra-VPC RTT is ~1ms that's ok for some models, but extra 1ms per token adds up. We generally keep KV local to runtime to avoid that. 07:05 Priya: Any requirements for subnet sizing? 07:10 Diego: For private deployments we need control-plane subnet(s) - small /27s for control plane ENIs often enough. For runtime worker subnets depending on model size and autoscaling, we recommend /22 or bigger - estimate 1-2 instances per /28 depending on instance type. We'll share terraform snippets. 07:30 Liam: And NAT throughput - if we use NAT Gateway for egress, can it be a bottleneck when pulling many large model shards? 07:38 Diego: Yes, NAT throughput matters. Best practice: use gateway endpoints for S3/ECR so artifact pulls don't hit NAT. If NAT is used, consider using multiple NAT gateways per AZ. 07:50 Maya: For private control plane, do we need cross-account peering? 07:55 Diego: No - PrivateLink avoids cross-account peering for control plane. For data plane, many customers prefer TGW or peering for high throughput. 08:05 Tom: On TLS termination - where does it happen? 08:10 Ava: We can terminate TLS at your side or at Redwood's ingress depending on model. For PrivateLink the connection is encrypted; mutual TLS optional. 08:20 Priya: KMS integration - can we use our KMS/HSM for model keys? 08:25 Diego: We support customer-managed keys for data at rest (S3) and can integrate with your KMS for encrypting logs/artifacts. For runtime-in-memory keys that's trickier; we can discuss HSM-based key wrapping for credential material. 08:40 Maya: Are there example architecture diagrams? 08:45 Ava: Yes, we'll include diagrams showing PrivateLink control plane, TGW data plane, gateway endpoints for S3/ECR, and sample route tables. 08:55 Liam: For benchmarking, what data should we provide? 09:00 Diego: Provide sample prompt sets, typical sequence lengths, concurrency targets, and a staging VPC with an endpoint we can reach. We'll run both synthetic and real prompts. 09:10 Maya: Ok we'll prepare that. 09:12 Tom: One last thing - how do you handle model rollouts and fallbacks in private deployments? 09:18 Diego: We have rollout policies: canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to a hosted-compatible variant if a runtime pool fails. In private VPC we still support rollouts controlled by the control plane. 09:30 Priya: Anything else on compliance? 09:32 Ava: We'll include SOC2 Type II report, ISO docs, pen test summaries, and details on audit log retention and redaction. 09:40 Maya: Great. let's capture next steps. 09:45 Ava: Recap: I'll send architecture + terraform snippets + security pack by Friday (Ava). Diego will prepare perf harness and run initial benchmarks once Helios provides staging VPC credentials or presigned artifact URLs. Helios to provide test data and confirm whether gateway endpoints will be used. 09:58 Tom: Thanks all. 09:59 Meeting ends.

Notes about transcript: transcription has occasional mislabels and filler words, some model names were abbreviated, "private link" and "PrivateLink" appear interchangeably.
